notes.short: Paul calls them “kings” to rebuke their pride
notes.about: Paul tells the Corinthians they already have all they want, are rich, and reign as kings without the apostles. He means the opposite: they only think so, and in their pride they look down on the men through whom they received the gospel. The next verses set the apostles' hardships beside them.

figure.name: Irony
figure.words: Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings.
figure.means: that they only think themselves full, rich and reigning, and are proud of gifts they received

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse as true Irony. Albert Barnes calls it irony and cutting sarcasm, and Calvin says Paul ridicules their self-complacency by irony and upbraids their ingratitude. Simon Browne (Matthew Henry's Commentary) hears a smart irony: they reign only in their own conceit. Adam Clarke judges it a strong irony. On the closing wish, Barnes hears it earnest and Bullinger ironic.
notes.limit: The note is on the first three sentences. Writers differ on the closing wish: some hear the irony go on, while others hear Paul's earnest wish that they truly were as blessed as they thought.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Human Irony, p. 813
cites.quote: This verse is true Irony. But other figures are involved.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: It is generally agreed that this is spoken in irony, and that it is an indignant sarcasm uttered against the false and self-confident teachers in Corinth. ... The whole passage is an instance of most pungent and cutting sarcasm ... But the more probable interpretation is, that Paul here drops the irony, and addresses them in a sober, earnest manner.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Having in good earnest, and without the use of any figure, beat down their vain confidence, he now also ridicules it by way of irony, because they are so self-complacent, as if they were the happiest persons in the world. ... he tacitly upbraids them with ingratitude, because they had the audacity to despise him, or rather those, through means of whom they had obtained everything.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He presses the duty of humility upon them by a very smart irony, or at least reproves them for their pride and self-conceit ... to intimate how much the Corinthians were elated by the abundance of their wisdom and spiritual gifts ... "You have reigned as kings," says the apostle, "that is, in your own conceit;

notes.short: Love is pictured as a person: patient and kind
notes.about: Paul speaks of love as if it were a person who is patient and kind and does not envy or boast. Giving love the ways of a person makes his account of it lively and moving.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: Love is patient, love is kind
figure.means: love, given the qualities and actions of a person, so that the account of it is lively and moving

notes.evidence: Benson says the apostle here gives love the qualities and actions of a person, to make his account of that divine grace the more lively and affecting.

cites.quote: Here the apostle attributes to love the qualities and actions of a person, in order to render his account of that divine grace the more lively and affecting.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: All they want, then rich, then kings: a climb
notes.about: The three sentences climb: from having all they want, to being rich, to reigning as kings, the highest step of all. Each claim goes beyond the one before it, which shows how highly the Corinthians thought of themselves.

lines.words: Already you have all you want.
Without us, you have become kings.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes calls the third clause a climax: men filled with food, then the rich, then men raised to a throne, the highest elevation. Simon Browne (Henry's Commentary) sees a gradation from sufficiency to wealth and thence to royalty; Calvin says Paul goes step by step, the last much more than the other two; J. A. Bengel calls full, rich, kings a gradation, each step with its own pride.

cites.quote: This is simply carrying forward the idea before stated; but in the form of a climax. The first metaphor is taken from persons “filled with food;” the second from those who are so rich that they do not feel their lack of more; the third from those who are raised to a throne, the highest elevation, where there was nothing further to be reached or desired.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: There is a very elegant gradation from sufficiency to wealth, and thence to royalty, to intimate how much the Corinthians were elated by the abundance of their wisdom and spiritual gifts
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He proceeds, too, step by step, in exposing their insolence. In the first place, he says, that they were full: this refers to the past. He then adds, Ye are rich: this applies to the future. Lastly, he says, that they had reigned as kings this is much more than either of those two.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: A gradation [ascending climax]: full, rich, kings. ... in consequence of fulness, they were fastidious; of opulence, they were insolent; of kingly power, they were proud.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/bengel/1_corinthians/4.htm

notes.short: Death is spoken to as a beaten foe
notes.about: Here the chapter breaks into a cry of triumph that speaks to Death as if it were a person, a foe armed with a sting, and asks where its victory and its sting have gone. At the resurrection, death's power to hurt is taken away.

figure.name: Apostrophe
figure.words: Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?
figure.means: Death, spoken to as a person: an enemy whose victory and sting are gone

original.note: In Paul's Greek “sting” is kentron, a point or goad, and the sting of a creature such as a bee or a scorpion.

notes.evidence: Bullinger, under Apostrophe to inanimate things, gives Hosea 13:14 and points to this verse. Clarke says Death is personified here, armed with a sting like a goad. Barnes says the sting is given to death personified, in language of exultation. Simon Browne (Matthew Henry's Commentary) says the saints glory over death as a vanquished enemy.
notes.limit: Some read the cry as Paul's own; others as the song the raised saints will sing over death.

cites.quote: “O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction.” See 1Co 15:55
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Both Death and Hades are here personified: Death is represented as having a sting, dagger, or goad, by which, like the driver of oxen, he is continually irritating and urging on

cites.quote: The word which is here rendered sting (κέντρον kentron) denotes properly a prick, a point, hence, a goad or stimulus ... It denotes here a venomous thing, or weapon, applied to death personified, as if death employed it to destroy life, as the sting of a bee or a scorpion is used. ... The language here is the language of exultation, as if that was taken away or destroyed.

notes.about: Paul answers the church's boasting with a saying he expects them to know: a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough. One sin left alone in the church, like the man living in sin among them, will spread and spoil the whole. Paul uses the same saying in Galatians 5:9 also.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough
figure.means: one sin, or one sinner, left alone will spread and corrupt the whole church

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia, or Proverb, among sayings first in Scripture. Adam Clarke calls it a common maxim and reads the leaven as the sinning man left in the church. Albert Barnes calls it evidently a proverbial saying: one sin allowed in the church spreads through it all. John Calvin says Paul uses a proverbial saying to show a whole multitude infected by one man.
notes.limit: Most of these writers treat it as a saying already in use; one places it among sayings first found in Scripture that later came into general use.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 765
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... “A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump.” Leaven is always used in a bad sense.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: do you not know and acknowledge the truth of a common maxim, a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump? notes.short: The Passover lamb pointed ahead to Christ
notes.about: Paul calls Christ “our Passover lamb.” The lamb Israel slew at Passover pointed ahead to Him. As Israel put away all leaven when the lamb was slain, so those for whom Christ has been sacrificed are to clear out the old leaven of sin.

figure.name: Type
figure.means: Christ, whom the lamb slain at Passover pictured ahead of time

original.note: In Paul's Greek the words are to pascha hēmōn, “our Passover”; the word pascha here means the Passover lamb.

notes.evidence: Barnes: no doubt the paschal lamb was a type of the Messiah, designed to typify Him; pascha usually means that lamb. Calvin: Paul explains the correspondence between the figure in the Passover and the reality, Christ sacrificed once. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): as the days of unleavened bread began with the slain lamb, so with Christ slain. Benson: the paschal lamb represented Christ.

cites.quote: There can be no doubt here that the paschal lamb was a type of the Messiah … Our "paschal lamb," for so the word πάσχα pascha usually signifies. … that that lamb was designed to adumbrate or typify him
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Paul, having it in view to exhort the Corinthians to holiness, shows that what was of old figuratively represented in the passover, ought to be at this day accomplished in us, and explains the correspondence which exists between the figure and the reality. … Christ, says Paul, is our Passover He was sacrificed once
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: as the Jews began the days of unleavened bread with the slaying of the Passover lamb, so, Christ our Passover having been already slain, let there be no leaven of evil in you who are the "unleavened lump."

notes.about: Paul says, “If my preaching is voluntary, I have a reward.” By voluntary he means without pay: the next verse speaks of offering the gospel free of charge. He uses the lesser word to say the greater thing. One writer finds this way of speaking suited to his self-denial.

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.means: preaching without pay, offering the gospel free of charge

original.note: In Paul's Greek the word is hekōn, willingly, set beside misthon, a reward: to preach for nothing and yet have a reward.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis (a belittling): Paul means gratuitously, but lessens the wording to increase his meaning. Bengel says willingly stands here for gratuitously, so that with a reward it makes an oxymoron, and that Paul, speaking of his own affairs, often heightens or lessens his words, a way suited to express his self-denial.

cites.quote: “For if I do this thing willingly, I have a reward.” He means gratuitously; but lessens the wording, so as to increase his meaning.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This is here used instead of gratuitously, whence I have a reward makes an oxymoron; ... Paul often, when speaking of his own affairs, uses increase and diminution ... not unlike a catachresis, and suitable to express his self-abnegation.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/bengel/1_corinthians/9.htm

notes.short: Man and woman, then woman and man, said twice
notes.about: Paul names man, then woman, and turns the pair around: “man did not come from woman, but woman from man.” Verse 9 makes the same turn: “Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.” Repeating the words in reverse order sets the two in contrast.

figure.name: Antimetabole
figure.words: man did not come from woman, but woman from man
figure.means: the man and the woman contrasted: the woman came from the man, not the man from the woman

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists verses 8 and 9 under Antimetabole, or Counterchange, which he defines as words repeated in reverse order to oppose one thing to another or to contrast two or more things. He sets out both turns: man and woman, then woman and man, in verse 8, and the same again in verse 9.
notes.limit: The note is about how the words are set out, not the whole teaching: verses 11 and 12 add that in the Lord “woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman.”

cites.quote: This figure repeats the word or words in a reverse order, for the purpose of opposing one thing to another, or of contrasting two or more things. ... a “For the man b is not of the woman; b but the woman a of the man. c Neither was the man created d for the woman, d but the woman c for the man. ”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: Paul calls himself least, and God's grace stands out
notes.about: Paul calls himself the least of the apostles, unworthy of the name, because he persecuted the church. He sets himself low, and God's grace stands out: “But by the grace of God I am what I am” (verse 10). Yet, defending his calling, he could say he was “in no way inferior” (2 Corinthians 11:5).

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.means: Paul lowers himself, so that the grace of God that made him an apostle is seen the greater

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis, the lowering of one thing to magnify another: it magnifies the grace of God in verse 10. Calvin says Paul gladly abased himself to magnify God's grace, and has him say he will be of no account so that God's goodness may shine the more. Simon Browne (Matthew Henry's Commentary) says Paul, the more he worked, grew humbler and readier to magnify God's favour.
notes.limit: One writer thinks Paul was also answering those at Corinth who belittled him; another adds that he was least because he was the last of the apostles to be called.

cites.quote: “I am the least of the apostles.” This is said to magnify the grace of God (verse 10). Whereas, when magnifying his claims, he could say to these same Corinthians, “I suppose I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: he was at all times voluntarily, and even cheerfully, disposed to abase himself, that he might magnify the grace of God, yet I suspect that in this instance he wished to obviate calumnies. ... there were some at Corinth that made it their aim to detract from his dignity ... I shall suffer myself to be of no account whatever, that the goodness of God towards me may shine forth the more.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He was highly favoured of God, but he always endeavoured to keep up a mean opinion of himself, and to express it. ...
